title: Deadline-based flush policy exploration
content:
Summary:

This is a working log for the deadline-based flush policy exploration. Goal: measure whether adding a soft per-request deadline (relative to arrival) as an additional flush trigger reduces tail latency (P99/P99.9) without materially hurting throughput or increasing mean latency for small interactive workloads.

Motivation and background:
- Continuous coalescing improves GPU throughput but can amplify long-tail latency when low-rate interactive requests wait behind large groups. Current heuristics use size/time thresholds (min_batch, max_wait_ms) and age-based priority, but we still see long isolated requests stuck for multiple scheduling rounds under heavy bursty traffic.
- Idea: treat each incoming request as carrying a soft deadline (deadline_ms). Scheduler enqueues normally but will force-flush any batch containing a request whose deadline is expired. Deadlines can be relative (arrival + d_ms) or absolute tied to SLO tiers. This aims to bound head-of-line blocking without aggressive preemption.

Hypotheses:
1) A per-request deadline (200ms–600ms) will reduce P99/P99.9 by up to 25% for mixed workload traces with low QPS tails.
2) Deadlines tuned to the workload's median inter-arrival will have minimal impact on overall throughput (<5% tokens/sec) if the kernel batching path tolerates variable sizes.
3) With fairness weighting (age weight + deadline penalty), the scheduler can retain high throughput while improving tail latencies for high-priority interactive traffic.

Testbed and baseline:
- Hardware: 8x A100 80GB nodes in dedicated test cluster (rt-bench-03).
- Runtime: latest main branch as of 2024-10-28 with kernel selection optimizations disabled to isolate scheduler effects.
- Baseline config: min_batch_size=8, max_batch_size=128, max_wait_ms=12, age_weight=1.0, no per-request deadline.
- Workloads: three representative traces collected from production: (A) interactive-chat (median tokens 40, QPS 18, bursty tail), (B) async-embeddings+chat mix (50/50 mix, variable token lengths), (C) evaluation-sim (uniform request sizes high token counts).
- Metrics captured: tokens/sec, request/sec, p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9 latency (inference-start-to-first-token and end-to-end), batch size distribution, GPU utilization, kernel occupancy, scheduler queue length, number of forced flushes, and QoS violations (missed SLOs).

Experiment matrix:
- Dimension 1: deadline_ms per request = {off, 200, 350, 500}
- Dimension 2: deadline mode: {relative-arrival, tiered-by-route}
- Dimension 3: fairness policy: {age-only, age+deadline-penalty(0.5), age+deadline-penalty(1.0)}
- Dimension 4: max_wait_ms = {6, 12, 20} (to see interaction with deadline)
- Run length: 30 minutes steady-state per condition after 5 minute warmup. 3 seeds each.

Instrumentation notes:
- Added per-request metadata field deadline_ts and traced it through the scheduler, coalescer, and runtime.
- Collected per-batch trace with timestamps for: first-arrival, batch-formation, kernel-start, kernel-end, response-write-start.
- Extended histograms for queueing-time per-request and per-batch-size breakdowns.
- Logging: every forced flush emits a short structured log: {batch_id, expired_deadlines: [count, examples], reason}.

Selected results (high level):
- Trace A (interactive-chat, bursty): deadline_ms=350, mode=relative-arrival, fairness=age+deadline-penalty(0.5), max_wait_ms=12
  - P99 reduced from 420ms (baseline) to 320ms (-24%).
  - P99.9 reduced from 820ms to 610ms (-25.6%).
  - Mean latency increased by 6% (mostly due to more small batches on forced flushes).
  - Tokens/sec drop ~3.4%. GPU occupancy variation increased slightly (stddev +2.1%).
  - Fraction of forced-flush batches: 11% of batches contained at least one expired deadline.

- Trace B (mixed): deadline_ms=200, relative, age-only fairness
  - P99 small improvement (~8%). Throughput drop ~5% for this aggressive deadline, and P50 unchanged.
  - Observed many more very-small batches (size <= 4) after forced flushes, kernel overhead increased.

- Trace C (long eval requests): deadlines had minimal effect (requests exceed deadline naturally) but introduced jitter in batch sizes; best to keep deadlines off for pure high-token evaluation workloads.

Observations and patterns:
- Sweet spot around 300–400ms for interactive traces given our current kernel warmup and seq lengths (median tokens 30–60). Below 250ms the forced flush overheads start to dominate and throughput drops >5%.
- Combining deadline with a modest deadline-penalty in fairness preserves opportunities to form larger batches for non-urgent traffic: age+deadline-penalty(0.5) consistently performed better than age-only or penalty=1.0.
- Increasing max_wait_ms to 20ms reduces number of forced flushes for the same deadline because the coalescer captures more arrivals; however, at high burstiness max_wait_ms causes higher tail if deadline is off. Interaction is non-linear.

Micro-profiling notes:
- Forced-flush batches tend to have more kernel invocation overhead per token: observed ~7–12% higher kernel overhead (kernel-start latency) for batches <8 compared to baseline 32-sized batches.
- KV cache hit rates unaffected; deadline mechanism is orthogonal to cache.
- Scheduling CPU overhead negligible (<1% cycles) but logging rate increases and needs rate-limiting for production.

Failure modes:
- Aggressive deadlines in mixed clusters cause throughput cliffs when the system frequently produces many small batches; this cascades into GPU underutilization and increased queuing behind heavy requests.
- When deadlines are tiered by route, misclassification or inaccurate route priority mappings caused interactive routes to starve if their configured deadlines were too long.

Operational implications:
- Defaulting to a conservative deadline (e.g., 350ms) for interactive tiers could improve customer-visible tail latencies without large throughput penalties. Make deadline opt-in per-route for Dedicated/Private customers.
- Expose deadline as a route-level configurable with fallback to global default in Console. Provide a tuning guide: start at 350ms, monitor P99 and tokens/sec, reduce to 200ms only if SLOs require tighter tail at cost of throughput.
- Add toggles to rate-limit forced-flush logs and a runtime metric for forced_flush_rate to feed into dashboards and alerts.

Next steps / action items:
- (Marco) Run an additional sweep with kernel-selection optimizations enabled to see if smaller-batch kernel paths mitigate throughput loss (JIRA-RT-6489). Target date: 2024-11-20.
- (Priya) Add route-level UI mock for deadline configuration in Console and solicit PM feedback. Draft due: 2024-11-18.
- (Evan) Create a lightweight aggregator that collapses forced-flush logs into one-per-minute summaries to reduce logging noise. Patch in PR 3187 needs review.
- Run longer-duration (6hr) soak with conservative deadline=350ms on canary cluster to validate no degradation during diurnal QPS patterns. Owner: Aisha. Target start: 2024-11-15.

Open questions:
- Should deadline be absolute (ms since arrival) or expressed as percentile-bound (e.g., <= target tail allowance)? Percentile approach may map better to SLOs but complicates per-request metadata.
- How should deadlines interact with bursty multi-tenant GPU nodes where opportunistic batching across tenants is possible? Is a cross-tenant deadline enforcement feasible?

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft and focuses on the scheduler-level changes only. We deliberately disabled kernel-selector autotuning for controlled measurements; real-world impact may be smaller once small-batch fast-paths are enabled.
- See linked artifacts for trace ids and the prototype PR. Please comment on: recommended default value, whether deadline should be exposed in hosted API vs console-only, and telemetry we should add for early warning of throughput cliffs.

Changelog:
- 2024-11-06 initial draft (Aisha)
- 2024-11-09 added instrumentation details and early results (Marco)
- 2024-11-12 added operational recommendations and next steps (Priya)
